---
title: "Quiz: domain shift"
---

Short questions on models that meet new microscopes. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Name three things that change between two microscopes and one that changes between two experiments on the same microscope.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Light, optics, camera; and the sample.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Microscopes: brightness and background (lamp, exposure, gain), blur and pixel size (objective, focus), noise (camera, exposure time), or the whole modality. Experiments: stain batch, cell line, treatment, the share of each cell class, confluence.
:::

---

**Q2.** How can you notice a shift before you have any labels of the new images?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare something you can compute on every image.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Compare statistics of the old and new images: intensity histograms, means and spreads of measured features or of a network's internal features. A large difference (in units of the old spread) signals a shift. The network's confidence is not a reliable signal: it can be confidently wrong.
:::

---

**Q3.** You standardise each microscope's intensities with its own mean and SD. When does this hurt?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What else moves the mean intensity?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the new images differ for a biological reason, e.g. fewer bright mitotic cells: their lower mean is real, but normalisation removes it and shifts every cell. In the demo: 83 % instead of 92 % with no microscope change at all.
:::

---

**Q4.** What does "re-estimating the normalisation statistics" of a network change, and what does it need?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which numbers are stored in a normalisation layer?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It replaces the stored means and variances of the normalisation layers by those measured on the new images; no weights are trained. It needs unlabelled images of the new microscope (enough for stable statistics), and it has the same trap as normalising the inputs.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is augmentation during training not a complete answer to domain shift?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which variations does the model see?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It only teaches invariance to the variations you simulate (gain, offset, blur, noise); a new modality or a new cell line is not one of them. And ignoring a variation that was informative (intensity) costs accuracy on the original images (96 % → 90 % in the demo).
:::

---

**Q6.** You fine-tuned your model on 20 labelled images of the new microscope and report 94 % on those 20 images. What is wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which images were used to adapt?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The test images were used for fine-tuning: the score is optimistic. Test on other images of the new microscope, from other wells or days, and report the old microscope's score separately too.
:::
